title: A Catholic doubter
hook: he remained Catholic and died during Mass in 1592, while doubting nearly everything else

segments.voice: Yesterday, the wars: Montaigne kept his gate open and said the same plain words to both sides. Your line was talk to both. Where did you keep your words the same? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-six.

A pair of scales, two pans hanging level. Montaigne took that image as his emblem, he says, with a short question to go with it: what do I know? The same man submitted his writing to the judgment of the Church he was born in. He put the doubt and the faith in the same book, and hid neither one. Readers still argue about him, and about what that question left room for. Today, how one person held both.
screen: `A PAIR OF BALANCED SCALES.` → `WHAT DO I KNOW?` → `AND STILL IN HIS CHURCH.`

segments.voice: First, the doubt. In the Apology for Raymond Sebond, Montaigne takes apart human confidence piece by piece. Our senses fool us. Our reason argues both sides of anything. Animals may know things we don't. Even the skeptics' own claim, I doubt, says too much, he thinks, because it sounds sure of itself. So he turns it into a question: what do I know? Second, the faith. In the essay Of prayers, he says he puts his thoughts forward as things to be explored, not as truths to be believed, and he submits them to the Church he was born in. He says he'd gladly see Christians use the Lord's Prayer at every turn. Third, how he holds them together, and here readers differ. Some read him as a sincere Catholic who thinks reason is too weak to reach God, so faith must come as a gift, not a proof. Some read the faith as a careful cover for a deeper doubt. Some say the honest answer is that we can't see inside him, which would suit him well. Fourth, the end. Tradition says Montaigne died while Mass was being said in his room: the doubter, at the end, inside the rite of his church. Whatever you make of him, he didn't think faith and doubt had to evict each other. He let them share a room. A scale doesn't need one pan empty to hang level.
screen: `OUR SENSES AND REASON FOOL US.` · `SUBMITTED TO THE CHURCH.` · `SINCERE, OR A COVER?` · `MASS SAID IN HIS ROOM.` · then, large: `FAITH AND DOUBT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold faith and doubt side by side. Sit, and let your hands rest open, one on each knee, like the two pans of a scale. In one hand, place something you trust, whatever that is for you: a person, a practice, a belief, the sun coming up. In the other, place a question you can't answer. Don't let either hand win. Just feel the weight of both. Breathe, and let the scale hang. The bell holds the time.
A Catholic doubter. Montaigne, who asked what do I know?, stayed in the Church he was born in, and tradition says he died during Mass. Today's word.
Your line: faith and doubt. Today, when a question comes up that you can't settle, let it sit beside what you trust without forcing either one out. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne differ on how to hold his doubt and his Catholic faith together: some read him as a sincere believer who thought reason could not reach God, others read the faith as a cover, and some leave the question open.

original.note: Montaigne's French, in the Latin alphabet: what do I know? his question in the Apology for Raymond Sebond, beside the image of a balance.

trapdoor: what you thought: a doubter can't really be a believer.
what it means: Montaigne doubted human reason deeply and still stayed in his church; readers argue over how he held both.
what a scholar hears: some read his skepticism as clearing room for faith as a gift rather than a proof; others read his piety as protective cover.

notes: The index hook gives a year (1592) for his death; under the claims rule the script gives no year, and frames the death during Mass as tradition, from an account by a friend after his death (Étienne Pasquier's letter). Confirm.
'His longest essay' for the Apology is not stated in the text itself; it is the usual description. Cut if the claims editor prefers.
Confirm that 2.12 says he had the device ('Que sais-je?') with a balance; the script says only that he took the image as his emblem.
'Called himself a son of the Church' paraphrases 1.56's submission to the Catholic, Apostolic and Roman Church; confirm the wording.
Three readings of his faith given without ranking (fideist, cover, unknowable).

Editor pass: fixed a count error ('three words' for the four-word English 'what do I know?'); cut 'brass', 'merchant', 'went to Mass', 'son of the Church' and 'his longest essay' (not in the cited texts); the death during Mass now rests only on 'tradition says', with no claim about who reported it.
